angle: This is a combo deck wearing a value engine's clothes: four signed kills that take every opponent from 40 to 0 at the same state-based-action check, and a one-mana artifact none of the 99 can destroy switches off three of them — so the whole issue teaches you to name the shape that still works instead of shopping for an answer you do not have.

teases: Line 011: unbounded, free, and you finish the game on 80 life
The mandatory loop that ought to be a draw — and the rule that says it isn't
Three of the four kills never name your commander. Stop protecting him.
Zero cards in the 99 destroy an artifact. Here is the kill that doesn't care.

departments.headline: THE CARD YOU NEVER HAVE TO DRAW
departments.dek: One card in this deck is exempt from variance, and a single rule says so. So what is that guarantee worth to a pilot whose three best kills never name him?
departments.body:
Begin with the clause that makes this format unlike every other one. CR 903.8: "A player may cast a commander they own from the command zone." Yawgmoth is therefore not a card you draw. He is a card you have. The simulation puts him on the battlefield in 9,846 of 10,000 games, mean turn 4.294, median 4, and 7,220 of those cast him on turn four exactly.

The price of the guarantee sits in the same rule, and it compounds: "an additional {2} for each previous time the player casting it has cast it from the command zone that game." Four mana, then six, then eight, then ten. Set that schedule beside mean available mana of 3.911 on turn four, 5.223 on turn six and 7.1 on turn ten. The holding is short. The first recast costs you a turn. The second costs you the whole turn. The third is a turn nobody at this table is going to give you.

Colour identity is CR 903.4 — "the color or colors of any mana symbols in that card's mana cost or rules text". One black symbol in his cost, one colour in the deck, and the mana audit has nothing to reconcile: black is 100% of the pip load and 100% of the sources, on curve at 95.5% once ramp is counted.

What that identity costs is breadth, and this issue is about the bill. The 99 holds no counterspell and not one card that destroys or exiles an artifact. Five tutors cannot find one, because there is none to find. That is the format's bargain stated as a rule rather than as a complaint.

Commander damage the record disposes of quickly. CR 903.10a removes a player "dealt 21 or more combat damage by the same commander over the course of the game". Yawgmoth is a 2/4 who would much rather be sacrificing than attacking, and 21 damage is eleven connections. Commander damage is a coincidence here, never a clock.

Now the clause to memorise, because it cuts both ways. CR 702.16b: "A permanent or player with protection can't be targeted by spells with the stated quality and can't be targeted by abilities from a source with the stated quality." Yawgmoth is a Human Cleric with protection from Humans, so his own ability can never target him — the 2/4 who could comfortably absorb four counters is not allowed to take one. The Counselor's files lean on that: once an opponent's creature is gone, every legal target is one of your own bodies, which is exactly what stops the grinding boards at seven or eight deaths. In the other direction it is free armour at a table thick with Human commanders.

One last fact about the zone. Four opponents can see it, and they cannot see your hand. What they price when this commander resolves is a reputation rather than a board — and the bracket sheet agrees with them, landing on floor 4 from four Game Changers and eleven two-card infinite records, inside a declared target of 4.

COACH'S READ. Here is the part that feels wrong and is right: do not buy the insurance. Three of your four signed kills name him nowhere. He is a draw engine, a second free outlet and a removal magnet, and you should be pleased to trade him. Cast him on curve, draw four or five cards, and let somebody spend a card on him. Do not hold mana to protect him and do not mulligan toward him. When you do want him back, notice which routes are not recasts at all: Malakir Rebirth and Supernatural Stamina return him to the battlefield, so the tax never advances, while Animate Dead and Victimize reach him in the graveyard. Price the second trip before you make the first — six mana spent getting him back is six mana not spent assembling.

captions.Malakir Rebirth // Malakir Mire: **A RESCUE IS NOT A RECAST:** it returns him to the battlefield, so the commander tax never advances — and the return is one more death trigger for every drain you have down.
captions.Lightning Greaves: **INSURANCE, NOT ARMOUR:** equip is sorcery speed, so the turn to arm him is the turn before you need him. Shroud cuts you off from your own tricks too.

pilot_tips.text: The best reason to have him on the battlefield is this card — free removal, exile rather than destroy, on any turn you spent assembling.

departments.headline: YOUR COMMANDER IS NOT THE PLAN
departments.dek: Three of the four signed kills never name Yawgmoth, and one of them costs you nothing at all. So what is he actually for on turns one through five?

callouts.title: BUY CHEAP, BUY EARLY
callouts.text: Your cheapest classes arrive first and they arrive on their own: a drain at a mean draw turn of 2.570, a free repeatable sacrifice outlet at 2.718, an ignition source at 2.802, renewable fodder at 2.859. Carrion Feeder, Viscera Seer, Fume Spitter, Bitterblossom and Reassembling Skeleton all cost one or two mana. Put them down and stop admiring them.

callouts.title: LAND HIM ON CURVE, THEN DRAW
callouts.text: The commander hits the battlefield on turn four in 7,220 of 10,000 goldfished games, mean 4.294, median 4, and 91.1% by turn six. From that turn on every spare body is a card — and the ability costs no mana at all, so you can hold it up on somebody else's turn for free.

callouts.title: HOLD THE PAYOFF
callouts.text: You draw some drain by turn ten in 82.4% of games unassisted. You draw Bastion of Remembrance specifically in 16.7%. Those are different facts. The class is deep, the card that loops in three of the four signed kills is one card, and a drain in hand is a surprise while a drain on the battlefield is a target.

callouts.title: NAME THE SHAPE BEFORE YOU GO
callouts.text: There are exactly four shapes. Warren Soultrader plus Gravecrawler plus an each-opponent drain. Gravecrawler plus Phyrexian Altar plus a second Zombie plus a drain. Exquisite Blood plus a body reading 'Whenever you gain life, each opponent loses 1 life.' Mikaeus plus your commander plus a non-Human body plus a drain. Extra creatures never move that answer.

captions.Yawgmoth, Thran Physician: **THE DRAW ENGINE:** 'Pay 1 life, Sacrifice another creature' has no mana anywhere in the cost, so no tax and no lock reaches it. Use him to draw for three or four turns before you use him for anything else.
captions.Gravecrawler: **THE HUB IN FURNITURE'S CLOTHES:** a one-mana 2/1 that cannot block, in a deck full of them — and the recursive half of both unbounded kills. Nobody spends removal on it. Deploy it turn one.
captions.Bastion of Remembrance: **THE PAYOFF THAT LOOPS:** the drain in three of the four signed kills, and an enchantment, so your own engine can never eat it and your own creature removal never has to.

pilot_tips.text: Play it on turn one and let the table file it as a body — the tell in this deck is never Gravecrawler, it is whatever you play beside it.
Cast it on turn two even with nothing to sacrifice; a body every upkeep for 1 life is the cheapest fodder you will ever buy.

departments.pull_quote: You are nothing, and then you are the whole table. There is no board in between.

departments.headline: ELEVEN GROUPS, AND THE ONE THAT ISN'T HERE
departments.dek: Read the first two groups and you know how this deck ends a game. Read to the end and you will notice the group nobody could write for it: the cards that destroy an artifact.

roster.role: The four kills — the cards that actually end games
The other drains — each opponent, or one
Free sacrifice outlets — 77.9% by turn ten
Renewable fodder — the bodies that come back
Mana that is not a land

callouts.title: TWO CARDS CARRY THREE KILLS
callouts.text: Gravecrawler is the recursive half of both unbounded loops; Bastion of Remembrance is the drain in three of the four. Each is one card, each is about 7% of an opening seven, and each turns up by turn ten in roughly one game in six unassisted — 16.5% and 16.7%. Five tutors are the only redundancy either of them has.

callouts.title: EACH OPPONENT, OR TARGET PLAYER
callouts.text: On the identical grinding board, a drain reading 'each opponent' removed 7 life from every seat — 28 across a four-opponent pod. Blood Artist, which reads 'target player loses 1 life', removed eight life in total. One word of templating, and the Counselor called the second one not a kill and not close.

callouts.title: THE GROUP WITH NO CARDS IN IT
callouts.text: Feed the Swarm is the only entry in the 99 that destroys or exiles a noncreature permanent an opponent controls, and it reads creature or enchantment. Artifact: zero cards. Land: zero cards. Fourteen entries here want your own graveyard intact, and the cheapest permanent that seals a graveyard is an artifact.

callouts.title: TWO CARDS THE TAXONOMY HAS NO PATTERN FOR
callouts.text: Role coverage is 97.5%. The two it misses are Plumb the Forbidden and Supernatural Stamina — an instant-speed answer to a wrath, and a two-mana trick that hands you an extra death trigger. Absence of a role is not absence of the function; read the card.

captions.Nest of Scarabs: **SETTLED ARITHMETIC:** the number of creatures you put counters on sets the number of triggers, and the counters on each of those creatures set that trigger's 'that many'. One proliferate across three counter-bearing creatures makes three Insects, not six.
captions.Grave Pact: **ONE ACTIVATION, FOUR BOARDS:** every sacrifice that feeds a drain also strips a creature from all four opponents. It is the deck's only repeatable answer to a creature it cannot target.
captions.Reassembling Skeleton: **THE PUREST BODY IN THE DECK:** {1}{B} from the graveyard, forever, asking nothing but mana. It never runs out and it never needs a board.

pilot_tips.text: Never plan to fund the recursion loops with it — colorless mana does not cast Gravecrawler for {B}. Use it as an outlet and for bulk mana.

departments.pull_quote: Thirty-two combo lines are fully contained in this list. Four of them are signed. Containment is a shortlist, never evidence.

departments.headline: SHAPE, NOT NAMES
departments.dek: You keep your first seven 81.8% of the time, so you get to be picky and you almost never have to be. The question is never which card you hold — it is whether the hand makes bodies and can spend one for free.

hands.why: Three lands is the modal kept hand — 3,640 of the simulator's keeps hold exactly three. This one already carries a free outlet, renewable fodder, an ignition source and an each-opponent drain: the four classes the model finds earliest, at mean turns 2.718, 2.859, 2.802 and 2.570. Nothing in it costs more than two.

Fast mana is the thinnest class on the sheet at 42.7% unassisted by turn ten, and 712 of 10,000 games cast the commander on turn two — every one of them opened like this. The Skeleton gives him something to eat the moment he lands, and the tutor turns a 1.1% kill into an 18.0% one.

All payoff, nothing underneath it. Mean available mana is 3.911 on turn four and 4.603 on turn five, so a six-drop and a five-drop with no enabler in front of them means you do nothing for half the game. Enablers dig toward payoffs; payoffs sit there until the engine exists.

This is a kill in your hand and it is still a ship. One land, no fast mana, and the second Zombie the Phyrexian Altar loop needs is not here — 1,401 of 10,000 first sevens hold exactly one land, and one land is a mulligan unless Sol Ring, Ancient Tomb or Dark Ritual is sitting beside it. Ship it and you will draw into a shape; keep it and you will watch one.

captions.Dark Ritual: **ONE BLACK INTO THREE:** a ritual is not a source and the audit never counts it as one. It buys a specific turn, so keep it for the turn that matters and spend it there.
captions.Skullclamp: **KEEPABLE ON ITS OWN:** one mana, and every 1/1 you make becomes two cards. It is the draw engine that still works on the turns your commander is answered.

pilot_tips.text: Never ship a hand for lacking him — he arrives on turn four in 7,220 of 10,000 games without any help from you.

departments.pull_quote: Two to five lands and a cheap enabler. Keep first seven 81.8%, mean 0.216 mulligans — the deck is not asking you to gamble.

departments.headline: PICK BEFORE YOU READ
departments.dek: Six mana and three payoffs in hand on the first board. A one-mana artifact and a tutor on the second. Commit out loud to both before you read a word of the Coach's answer.
departments.pull_quote: Stop asking which payoff is biggest. Ask which one is still on the battlefield next turn.
departments.note: EDITOR: both spreads render from decisions/ and both boards are drawn entirely from the current 99. The kicker, headline, dek and pull quote are deliberately non-telegraphing because dept_furniture prints above the spreads — nothing above names a recommended branch.

departments.headline: FOUR WAYS TO END A TABLE
departments.dek: Ten scenarios went to the Counselor and ten came back signed. Four of them take every opponent from 40 to 0 at one state-based-action check. The other six exist to tell you which boards only look like they do.

callouts.title: KILL ONE: IT PAYS FOR ITSELF
callouts.text: Warren Soultrader, Gravecrawler and Bastion of Remembrance. Gravecrawler's own ability modifies the zone it may be cast from, so the permission is live in the graveyard every iteration, with the Zombie condition met by Soultrader — whom the loop never eats, because the cost says 'another creature'. Each activation's Treasure exactly funds the next cast. Per iteration: your life net 0 with a floor of 39, each opponent −1. Unbounded. Line 009.

callouts.title: KILL TWO: IT PAYS NOTHING AT ALL
callouts.text: Swap the Treasure for Phyrexian Altar and the loop gets cleaner. The Altar's ability needs no target and could add mana, so it is a mana ability and never uses the stack — it cannot be responded to, and its {B} is in your pool before anyone gets priority. Carrion Feeder holds the Zombie condition and is never the sacrifice. Each lap is +1 life for you and −1 for every seat. Thirty-nine more laps put all four at 0 together and you finish at 80. Line 011.

callouts.title: KILL THREE: MANDATORY, AND NOT A DRAW
callouts.text: Exquisite Blood beside a body reading 'Whenever you gain life, each opponent loses 1 life.' Neither card says 'may', so the loop is compulsory — and the Counselor's favourite question is whether that makes it a draw. It does not: a draw needs a sequence that could be repeated indefinitely, and every cycle here takes a life from every opponent, so there is a way to stop. Drain 40 takes all four from 1 to 0 at once. Line 012.

callouts.title: KILL FOUR: LETHAL, AND FINITE
callouts.text: Mikaeus grants undying, and your commander's −1/−1 counter does not shrink an undying body — it annihilates the +1/+1 undying left behind and re-arms the creature to die again. The counter is a reset, not a shrink. But the commander's draw is mandatory, so your library is the clock: 39 further activations needed against the 59 it permits, a margin of 20. Line 010.

callouts.title: THE BOARD THAT LOOKS LIKE A KILL
callouts.text: Your commander plus Nest of Scarabs plus a death-metered drain is bounded by bodies, and protection from Humans is why: he cannot target himself, so once the opponent's creature is gone every legal target is one of your own tokens. Seven drains, 28 life removed from a four-opponent pod, and your own total going up. A value engine that draws you cards. No ordering makes it a kill.

callouts.title: ONE WORD, AND THE POD SURVIVES
callouts.text: Blood Artist reads 'target player loses 1 life' where the drains that close games read each opponent. On that same bounded board: eight creature deaths, eight triggers, eight life removed of a pod's 160, with an exhaustive search of the line space finding nothing better. Refuted as a kill, and not narrowly. Play him as reach, never as the finish.

callouts.title: THREE EDGES WORTH CARRYING TO THE TABLE
callouts.text: Gaining zero is not gaining — an Insect killed by its own counter dies at toughness 0, so a lifegain drain sees nothing and eight death triggers pay only seven times. Entering counts as putting — a creature that arrives already wearing a −1/−1 counter does trigger Nest of Scarabs. And one activation can pay a drain twice: the sacrifice is a cost paid while the ability is already topmost, so a creation-and-sacrifice drain collects on both halves.

captions.Phyrexian Altar: **IT NEVER USES THE STACK:** a mana ability resolves on activation, so the {B} that recasts Gravecrawler is in your pool before anyone can respond. That is what makes this line free and uncounterable.
captions.South Wind Avatar: **FOUR TOUGHNESS, FOUR ACTIVATIONS:** on the bounded board its size buys the last activations. And a token that dies at toughness 0 gains you nothing, so it drains nobody — gaining zero is not gaining.
captions.Blood Artist: **REFUTED, NOT DEMOTED:** eight life in total against the 28 an each-opponent drain removes from the identical board. He is still a fine body that pays you for every death; he is simply not the drain you fetch.

pilot_tips.text: Do not spend her mid-loop under Mikaeus — her sacrifice places no counter, and only your commander's counter can strip an undying return, so the spare activation costs you a body for good.

departments.pull_quote: Forty drain events take a seat to zero. One has already resolved. Thirty-nine more, and nobody is left to respond.

departments.headline: NOTHING, THEN EVERYTHING
departments.dek: There is no board where you are lethal on one seat and merely scary to the rest. So what do four opponents actually read off your permanents — and how do you spend the misread?

callouts.title: THREAT WINDOW: THE SHAPE, NOT THE SWARM
callouts.text: The table counts creatures. Goldfish has you at a mean of 3.903 bodies by turn six, which reads as a fair little swarm and is not the plan. The board that ends the game is two to four specific permanents, and nobody at a Commander table audits permanents for a shape. Let them count.

callouts.title: THREAT WINDOW: MIKAEUS RESOLVES
callouts.text: He is half of seven of the eleven two-card infinite records the bracket sheet names, so he draws exile on sight from anyone who reads. He is also attached to your slowest kill — 39 activations needed against the 59 your mandatory draw permits. Cast him on a turn you want removal spent, and be pleased when it is.

callouts.title: THE PERMANENT YOU CANNOT BUY BACK
callouts.text: Grafdigger's Cage, Null Rod and Cursed Totem each switch off part of this machine, and nothing in the 99 destroys or exiles an artifact. So stop shopping for an answer you do not have: switch shapes that turn, and make somebody else's artifact removal the one thing you buy with real currency. Overpay for it. It is cheaper than the game you lose staring at a permanent you cannot touch.

callouts.title: SAY IT STRAIGHT AT RULE ZERO
callouts.text: Bracket floor 4, Optimized, forced independently by four Game Changers — Ancient Tomb, Demonic Tutor, Necropotence, Vampiric Tutor — and by eleven two-card infinite records, against a declared target of 4. Then the sentence that matters: four rules-verified kills, two of them unbounded and one a mandatory loop that ends only by killing the pod, each of the four ending every opponent at once. Nobody can turn that into a turn number, and you have told them the truth.

captions.Grave Pact: **THE ROOM-CHANGER:** a drain takes life quietly; an edict takes a creature from four players in front of everybody, every time a body of yours dies. Expect to be priced on the edicts, not the drains.
captions.Exquisite Blood: **IT DOES NOTHING THE TURN IT LANDS:** which is exactly why it resolves. Deploy the lifegain body first — a 3/4 deathtouch or a two-mana cleric reads as fair — and let the enchantment look like a lifegain card.
captions.Necropotence: **WHAT ACTUALLY TAKES YOUR LIFE:** not the engine. This, Bitterblossom, Black Market Connections, City of Brass and Ancient Tomb. Two of the signed loops finish you at 80.

pilot_tips.text: Equip at sorcery speed the turn before you need it — after the removal is announced it is decoration.

departments.pull_quote: You get no warning turn, so neither does the table. Sequence the loud half last and present at the end step before your own.

departments.headline: WHO ACTUALLY BEATS YOU
departments.dek: It is not the wrath — the wrath pays you four different ways. It is a one-mana artifact. So read every box below for the same thing: which of your four kills does this seat leave alive?

threats.read: Be visibly happy here. A wrath touches none of your kills: the critical permanents in every signed line are noncreature, and the board they blow up is decoration. Meanwhile Bastion of Remembrance, Zulaport Cutthroat and The Meathook Massacre bill every opponent when a creature of yours dies, and your rebuild is structural rather than held. Hold two mana whenever the control seat untaps with four or more open, and let Plumb the Forbidden turn their announcement into your draw step.

This is the seat that actually beats you, and it costs them one mana. Grafdigger's Cage stops the Gravecrawler recasts, so both unbounded loops go with it. Null Rod takes Phyrexian Altar and your Treasure. Cursed Totem takes the commander and every creature outlet you own. Nothing in the 99 answers any of them, so do not go shopping — learn which kill survives which and tutor for that one. Cage and Null Rod both leave Exquisite Blood; Cursed Totem leaves the Phyrexian Altar loop, which sacrifices with an artifact.

Recount your hand under a tax, never your board. Three of the four kills need essentially no external mana once assembled — line 009's Treasure funds the next cast, line 011's Altar refunds its own black, line 012 spends nothing — and the commander's ability costs no mana in the first place. Your window of weakness is deployment, not operation, so deploy under the tax as if this were the last turn you get.

You are the pod's stabiliser and you should stop apologising for the sweepers. Four scalable wipes, bodies to chump or eat, and Grave Pact converting every death you were causing anyway into a table-wide edict. Point the commander's counters at their creatures whenever a legal target exists — on the grinding board an opposing two-toughness body extended the engine by two activations rather than ending it. And spend life early: two of the signed loops finish you at 80.

Your hardest seat, so meet it head-on rather than hedge. You cannot interact on the stack at all, and every instant you hold points at a creature. Hold nothing: against combo the last profitable moment for an answer is now. Deadly Rollick is free while your commander is out, and Snuff Out is free with a Swamp. Then race with the shape you can finish — Exquisite Blood assembles at a mean turn of 5.301, faster than either recursion kill.

It earns its own box because it hits you unevenly, and knowing which half stays live is worth a whole game. Lines 009 and 011 cast Gravecrawler out of the graveyard every single lap, so a Rest in Peace effect blanks both unbounded loops. Line 012 touches no graveyard at all, and its signed board holds an empty one. Abandon the recursion plan on the spot and go get Exquisite Blood plus a body reading 'Whenever you gain life, each opponent loses 1 life.' Do not treat Mikaeus as a safe harbour on the way there — undying returns a creature from your graveyard too.

captions.Plumb the Forbidden: **THE WRATH, CONVERTED:** sacrifice any number of creatures as an additional cost and copy it once for each — their announcement becomes your draw step, and every sacrifice fires whatever drain you have down.
captions.Feed the Swarm: **THE WHOLE ANSWER TO A CLASS:** the only card in the 99 that destroys a noncreature permanent an opponent controls, and it reads creature or enchantment. A resolved artifact aimed at you has no answer in this library.

pilot_tips.text: Bank it — it enters tapped anyway, so play it on the turn their graveyard matters rather than the turn it is convenient.

departments.pull_quote: Interaction slots are the price of the engine. You paid it, and the bill arrives as an artifact you cannot remove.

departments.headline: WISH FOR THE KILL, NOT THE ENGINE
departments.dek: Your enabler classes turn up on their own in three games out of four. Your kills do not — so what is a tutor actually buying, and which single card completes two of them?

callouts.title: NEVER WISH FOR A CLASS YOU ALREADY GET
callouts.text: By turn ten, with no tutor involved: a drain 82.4%, a free repeatable sacrifice outlet 77.9%, renewable fodder 73.6%, an ignition source 73.1%. A wish lifts those to 94.1%, 92.0%, 90.0% and 90.0%. That is twelve to seventeen points on something the deck was handing you anyway.

callouts.title: THE KILLS ARE WHAT MOVES
callouts.text: Exquisite Blood's pairing goes 6.9% to 42.5%. The Mikaeus line 4.6% to 33.7%. The Soultrader loop 1.1% to 18.0%. The Phyrexian Altar loop 0.5% to 12.3%. Six-fold, seven-fold, sixteen-fold, twenty-four-fold — that is the entire job of these five cards.

callouts.title: POINT IT AT THE CARD IN THE MOST LINES
callouts.text: A wish on Gravecrawler completes two unbounded kills. A wish on Bastion of Remembrance completes the payoff half of three. A wish on Warren Soultrader or Phyrexian Altar completes exactly one. The fetch priority is arithmetic, not taste.

callouts.title: KNOW YOUR OWN CAP
callouts.text: Beseech the Mirror's bargained free cast stops at mana value 4. It reaches Gravecrawler, Carrion Feeder, Starscape Cleric, Bastion of Remembrance, Warren Soultrader, Phyrexian Altar, Marauding Blight-Priest, Grave Pact and South Wind Avatar. It never reaches Exquisite Blood at 5 or Mikaeus at 6 — those two belong to Demonic Tutor.

captions.Diabolic Intent: **THE COST THAT ISN'T:** the creature you sacrifice is a drain trigger with any payoff down, an edict with Grave Pact, and an undying return under Mikaeus. Pay it with a token, never with a piece.
captions.Demonic Tutor: **NO CONDITIONS, NO CEILING:** the only wish that does not care what the card costs, which makes it the only route to Exquisite Blood or Mikaeus on curve.
captions.Vampiric Tutor: **AN APPOINTMENT, NOT AN ARRIVAL:** it lands on top, so fire it at the end step before your own turn and the transit costs you nothing.

pilot_tips.text: Cast both Spree modes at once and point the draw at yourself — the search resolves first, so you draw exactly what you just booked.

departments.pull_quote: You are not tutoring to make this deck function. You are tutoring to convert.

departments.headline: ONE COLOUR, NOTHING TO RECONCILE
departments.dek: Pip share and source share cannot disagree when there is only one colour to be short of. So the audit narrows to a single number — and the yardstick it is measured against is not reachable in a deck built like this one.

callouts.title: THE YARDSTICK YOU CANNOT HIT
callouts.text: The model wants 36 black sources for a 90% on-curve rate. Thirty-four of your 36 land copies make black — Ancient Tomb and Urborg are the two that do not — so lands alone land at 88.2%. The audit says it plainly: in a deck this size the target is a yardstick, not a possibility.

callouts.title: EIGHT NONLAND PRODUCERS CLOSE IT
callouts.text: Agadeem's Awakening, Arcane Signet, Dark Ritual, Deadly Dispute, Malakir Rebirth, Phyrexian Altar, Pitiless Plunderer and Warren Soultrader all make black, lifting the count to 42 sources and on-curve black to 95.5%. Sol Ring and Ashnod's Altar make none: they buy speed, never fixing. Restricted mana anywhere in the 99 — none.

callouts.title: MOST OF THE RAMP IS NOT RAMP
callouts.text: Eleven ramp copies, and four of the eight coloured producers are sacrifice engines first and mana second. That is why the simulation separates engine mana — the class that turns a creature death into castable black — at 61.9% by turn ten from fast mana at 42.7%. They are different resources and they buy different turns.

callouts.title: TWO LANDS THE COUNT TREATS ODDLY
callouts.text: Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth produces no mana of its own and therefore counts for zero sources, while making every land in the game a Swamp. Cabal Coffers counts as exactly one source and taps for {B} per Swamp you control, beside 22 basics. One source is the accounting, not the experience.

captions.Swamp: **TWENTY-TWO OF THEM:** the untapped backbone, the reason Snuff Out costs four life instead of four mana, and the multiplier under Cabal Coffers. In mono-black the basic is one of the best cards in the deck.
captions.Phyrexian Tower: **A LAND THAT SACRIFICES:** a free outlet that makes {B}{B} while it does it. Where a spare body is a resource, this is one of the best untapped lands you can draw.

pilot_tips.text: Play it before Cabal Coffers, not after — every land you already control becomes a Swamp the Coffers can count.

departments.pull_quote: Seventy-five black pips across 55 cards, up to three in a single cost — and the first one is demanded on turn one.

departments.headline: THE ENGINE ARRIVES. THE KILL IS FETCHED.
departments.dek: Ten thousand openings, one fixed seed, no opponents and no interaction. The gap between the enabler bars and the kill bars is this deck's whole personality — and there is one number in here we refuse to print.

callouts.title: READ EVERY BAR AS A PAIR
callouts.text: The first figure excludes tutors entirely; the second lets one drawn, affordable tutor fill a single missing requirement. By turn ten: a drain 82.4% / 94.1%. A free repeatable sacrifice outlet 77.9% / 92.0%. Renewable fodder 73.6% / 90.0%. An ignition source 73.1% / 90.0%. Engine mana 61.9% / 85.1%. A tutor itself, 60.6%.

callouts.title: FOUR KILLS, FOUR NUMBERS
callouts.text: Exquisite Blood plus a lifegain drain 6.9% / 42.5%, mean turn 5.301 — the fastest. Mikaeus plus the commander 4.6% / 33.7%. Warren Soultrader plus Gravecrawler plus a drain 1.1% / 18.0%. Gravecrawler plus Phyrexian Altar plus a second Zombie plus a drain 0.5% / 12.3%. Several of these components rest on one named card, and a named card is about 7% of an opening seven.

callouts.title: THE NUMBER THAT DOES NOT EXIST
callouts.text: There is no union. The simulator scores each requirement group on its own, so a hand holding Exquisite Blood, Gravecrawler and Zulaport Cutthroat would satisfy three groups while assembling no kill at all. Nothing on this sheet means 'any kill assembled', we will not compute one, and you should not add these four together either.

callouts.title: THE COMMANDER'S HISTOGRAM
callouts.text: Turn four in 7,220 games of 10,000, mean 4.294, median 4, and on the battlefield by turn six in 91.1%. Turn two happens 712 times, every one of them off fast mana. He never arrives at all in 154.

callouts.title: THE BAR THAT NAMES THE PROBLEM
callouts.text: An answer to a noncreature permanent, drawn by turn ten: 17.3%. That is one card, Feed the Swarm, and it reaches creature or enchantment only. Every other bar on this sheet measures how well the engine turns up. This one measures what happens when somebody turns it off.

callouts.title: WHAT THE SIMULATION IS NOT
callouts.text: It models resource development, not games. No opponents, no removal, no politics, and a target counts as assembled the moment the cards are drawn rather than cast and protected. Read every bar as a floor on what turns up, never as a prediction of what happens.

departments.pull_quote: Four kills. Four numbers. Adding them would be the only lie in this issue.

departments.headline: BUY ANSWERS, NOT A FIFTH KILL
departments.dek: Seven of the ten answer a permanent this deck cannot touch, two widen the one kill a graveyard lock leaves alive, and the tenth closes nothing at all and says so on the page. Not one of them is here to make the engine bigger.

callouts.title: THE AXIS THAT ACTUALLY BINDS
callouts.text: Interaction-breadth reads 2 answered classes against a target of 5. Read across all seventy-nine entries and it is narrower than that sounds: artifact and land are literally zero. Feed the Swarm is the whole answer to a noncreature permanent, and it is in your hand 17.3% of the time by turn ten.

callouts.title: WIDTH MOVES FOUR NUMBERS AT ONCE
callouts.text: Three of the four kills share a drain slot. Widen that class and four separate assembly rates move on one purchase; add a fifth independent kill and one number moves. That is why this list ranks a redundant drain above a new combo every time.

callouts.title: NOT ONE LINE ON THIS PAGE IS SIGNED
callouts.text: Every combo a pick would open carries 'needs a stack scenario' by construction. Two are worth a resolve run before anything else: Bloodthirsty Conqueror beside Marauding Blight-Priest, because the whole case for that rank is that it substitutes for Exquisite Blood; and Reassembling Skeleton plus Phyrexian Altar plus Pawn of Ulamog, because every card in it bar the Pawn is already sleeved.

callouts.title: WHAT THE LIST DECLINED, AND WHY
callouts.text: Vito and Sanguine Bond each make a recorded infinite with Exquisite Blood and each read 'target opponent' — they kill one seat. Spine of Ish Sah and Lux Cannon reach every class this deck cannot, at seven mana and at three untap steps, and three turns of charging under a lock is a lost game. And symmetric graveyard hate is a liability here, not an upgrade: fourteen entries want your own graveyard intact.

captions.Feed the Swarm: **THE CARD THE WHOLE PAGE IS ABOUT:** one sorcery, creature or enchantment, and it is the deck's entire answer to a noncreature permanent. Everything ranked here is measured against how much of that gap it closes.

departments.pull_quote: Bracket floor 4 is already forced twice over, and every candidate here leaves it at 4. Judge each one on whether it answers a permanent you currently cannot touch.

departments.headline: TEN FILES, EVERY QUOTE VERBATIM
departments.dek: Ten complete resolutions, each citation reproduced exactly as the Comprehensive Rules prints it, with the checker's verdict as case status. This is the section that makes everything before it worth believing.
departments.pull_quote: Four of these ten files are kills. The other six exist to settle exactly what a board does before you bet a game on it.

departments.headline: SIXTY-EIGHT HANDS, NO HEADLINER
departments.dek: Nobody painted more than two cards in this deck and eleven artists are tied at exactly that, so there is no standout and we are not going to invent one. The feature goes to the pair whose two cards are the fastest kill and a wish that just misses it.

featured.note:
Start with the number that decides this section. Seventy-nine cards counted, sixty-eight different signatures, and the deepest single credit is two cards — eleven artists are tied there. Nobody dominates this deck, so nobody is going to be told they did.

Cynthia Sheppard is one of the eleven, and her pair is the one worth stopping on: Exquisite Blood and Beseech the Mirror. One is the enchantment half of the kill that assembles earliest, at a mean turn of 5.301 and the only one a graveyard lock leaves alive. The other is a tutor that can never free-cast it — Exquisite Blood is mana value 5 and the bargain stops at 4. One hand painted the card you want most and the wish that misses it by one.

One figure needs saying out loud, because it is the one that lies. Jorge Jacinto's Swamp appears twenty-two times here and counts once. Authorship is per card, never per copy — count it the other way and a basic land wins this section every single issue. Copies across the whole deck: 100.

The printings cluster where recent Commander product does. Twelve cards from Lorwyn Eclipsed Commander, eight from Secrets of Strixhaven Commander, seven from Tarkir: Dragonstorm Commander, five from Commander Masters. Nobody curated that, and the analysis is specific about it: there is no contiguous collector-number run anywhere in the deck, so nothing here was bought whole as a sealed product and shuffled in. It is simply where the cardboard comes from, and it is most of why no single hand gets ahead.

And nothing here is foil and nothing is borderless. This is a working deck, sleeved at working prices, and it looks like one on purpose.

also_worth_noting.note: Animate Dead and Ashnod's Altar — the reanimation spell and the free outlet, both still doing precisely what they did when they were printed.
Grave Pact and Massacre Girl, Known Killer. One hand, two cards, and both of them make somebody else's board smaller.
Stitcher's Supplier and The Meathook Massacre — the one-drop that fills your graveyard, and the wipe that bills the table while it empties the board.
Butcher Ghoul and Supernatural Stamina — a body that dies twice on its own, and the trick that makes any body die twice.
Black Sun's Zenith and Skullclamp — the sweeper that leaves counters your Nest of Scarabs can read, and the equipment that turns each 1/1 into two cards.

rhythm_notes: Act I opens on instruction (The Command Zone, one hero image and a tax ladder), climbs to the issue's narrative high in The Game Plan, then drops to the lowest-effort page in the book — The 99, eleven roster groups you browse rather than read. Act II is the climb: practice in Keep or Ship, active participation across two decision spreads in What's Your Play?, and The Kill as the mid-book peak, carrying the heaviest furniture in the issue (seven callout-steps plus ten signed spreads) exactly where the reader has the most momentum. Act III runs single-voice and medium the whole way — reflection, then reference, then instruction — which is the deliberate long breather after the peak; Table Manners sits between the two heaviest coaching sections so the six threat boxes in Know Your Enemy are never the reader's second dense spread in a row. Act IV carries the issue's only dense adjacency, Sources Say (analysis) into By the Numbers (analysis), and it is legal because the renderer emits its declared full-bleed art break between them; The Short List then drops to imagination and is the trough before the appendix. Act V descends cleanly: Judge's Desk is opt-in deep reference with one component and no callouts, Featured Artist is the palate cleanser, the Back Page closes. Furniture is thinnest where intensity is lowest — Judge's Desk carries a pull quote and nothing else, The Short List one caption and no tips.
gaps: PRESENTATION GATE, RESOLVED AND WORTH RESTATING: thirteen scenarios cleared the checker and ten of them describe a board this 99 can make. The other three resolve boards holding cards that are not in the deck, so `presentable` withholds them and the renderer shows ten. Every count in this plan — ten files, four kills, six other findings — is written against the ten. If a future artifact change makes one presentable again, the copy in The Kill, Judge's Desk and the cover violator must move together.

STACK SCENARIOS WORTH SPAWNING, RANKED: (1) The Meathook Massacre as a fourth substitute drain in the two recursion loops, which would widen the slot three signed kills already share and is the single highest-leverage unresolved question on the deck; (2) Exquisite Blood beside Marauding Blight-Priest or Starscape Cleric, since both carry the identical clause but neither gains life by itself while the signed board ignited from South Wind Avatar's own dies-trigger; (3) whether a resolved Grafdigger's Cage really does stop the Gravecrawler recasts and the undying returns — three of the four kills and most of this issue's political advice rest on an oracle-text reading nobody has checked; (4) the bare Mikaeus two-card records, seven of the eleven forcing the bracket floor and none of them resolved; (5) Grave Pact under a signed loop, because no file has ever measured the edicts.

THIN BUT HONEST — FEATURED ARTIST: there is no standout at all. The lead credit is two cards and eleven artists are tied there, so the section runs as a breadth feature with an authored pick from among the eleven. The note says plainly that no product was bought whole, that no contiguous collector-number run exists, and that the twenty-two Swamps count once. No taste is implied that the analysis cannot support.

THE SHORT LIST IS FORWARD-LOOKING ONLY: ten cards worth knowing about, ranked against measured holes, with no ownership question anywhere on the page. Every line any of them would open is a candidate — 'needs a stack scenario' — and the copy says so twice.

TIER DISCIPLINE: the four kills are ✓ and are stated as fact with their line numbers. Every assembly percentage in this plan is ◆ and phrased as a draw rate, never a win rate. The thirty-two contained combo lines and eleven two-card infinite records are named as containment, never as evidence. The Command Zone's coaching block is fenced under COACH'S READ so no ★ judgment sits inside the ✓ rules paragraphs.

STRATEGY DB HOLES THIS ISSUE WROTE AROUND: the corpus has no aristocrats section — no outlet / fodder / payoff triad, which is this deck's entire architecture; no vocabulary for what BOUNDS an iterative engine (library, bodies, or nothing at all — this issue has one of each); nothing pricing a recursive copy above a one-shot one, which is the whole reason Gravecrawler has no substitute; nothing treating mana-free or self-funding lines as a class, which is this deck's best property under a tax; and nothing on how to read several partially-overlapping win conditions as one probability, which is why By the Numbers has to decline rather than compute.

PUN BUDGET: three, all in furniture — 'THE HUB IN FURNITURE'S CLOTHES', 'THE COST THAT ISN'T', and the headline 'SIXTY-EIGHT HANDS, NO HEADLINER'. None sits inside a rules explanation or a data caption.
